finance.title: Inside 'Pig Butchering,' the Investment Scam That Cost Americans $7.2 Billion Last Year
finance.author: Maria Torres
finance.metaDescription: The FBI's 2025 IC3 report recorded $20.9 billion in cyber fraud losses, the worst year on record, driven largely by 'pig butchering' crypto investment scams.

body.text: How the Con Actually Works

The name itself tells you what the scam is built to do. Pig butchering, translated from the Chinese phrase sha zhu pan, describes a long-running confidence scheme in which a stranger builds what feels like a genuine friendship or romance with a victim, over weeks or, often, months, before eventually steering that relationship toward a cryptocurrency investment opportunity. The victim is the pig, deliberately fattened up with attention, trust, and fabricated investment gains, before ultimately being butchered for everything they're willing to put in.

What makes the con so effective is its patience and its production values. Victims are typically directed to professional-looking platforms designed to resemble legitimate cryptocurrency exchanges, complete with realistic account dashboards, functioning customer support chat windows, and fake profit displays that grow convincingly over time, all engineered to maintain the illusion of a real, working investment right up until a victim tries to actually withdraw their money.
The Worst Year on Record

The scale of the damage is no longer anecdotal. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center released its 2025 annual report in April 2026, documenting the worst year on record for cyber-enabled fraud in the United States: $20.877 billion in total reported losses across more than 1 million complaints, a 26% increase over the prior year. Within that total, investment fraud specifically accounted for $8.648 billion in losses, the highest-loss fraud category in the country for a fourth consecutive year, and cryptocurrency investment fraud, the category dominated almost entirely by pig butchering schemes, made up $7.228 billion of that figure on its own.

Cryptocurrency scams overall, a broader category encompassing pig butchering alongside other crypto-related fraud, cost Americans $11.37 billion in 2025, a 22% jump from the year before. The average pig butchering victim loses roughly $177,000 over the course of the scheme, a figure that reflects just how much time and psychological investment scammers put into building a target's trust before ever asking for money.
Who's Actually Being Targeted

The demographic pattern behind these losses cuts against the usual assumptions about who falls victim to online fraud. FBI data shows pig butchering victims skew disproportionately toward working professionals ages 30 to 49, people with genuine disposable income and, often, real financial sophistication, not the stereotypically less tech-savvy targets many people picture when they think about online scams. Older Americans remain heavily targeted too, and the losses there are especially severe: people aged 60 and older accounted for $4.35 billion of 2025's crypto scam losses, roughly 38% of the total, and elder fraud losses across all internet crime categories jumped 59% in a single year.

Behind those numbers sit real, often devastating personal consequences that don't always make it into the coverage. Under the FBI-run Operation Level Up, a proactive outreach initiative that contacts identified victims before they lose everything, 93 victims have been referred to an FBI victim specialist specifically for suicide intervention, a stark reminder that the financial toll of these schemes is often inseparable from serious psychological harm.
Why AI Is Making the Scam Harder to Spot

The FBI added AI as a formal crime descriptor to its reporting for the first time in the 2025 report, logging 22,364 AI-related complaints and $893.3 million in associated losses. Within pig butchering operations specifically, scammers are increasingly using AI-generated deepfake video calls to make a fabricated relationship feel more convincing and harder to question, and specialized criminal services now use AI to generate realistic synthetic identity documents and even conduct live know-your-customer verification interviews using deepfake technology, letting fraudulent accounts pass verification checks at legitimate cryptocurrency exchanges that were specifically designed to stop that kind of fraud.
Law Enforcement Is Fighting Back, With Real but Limited Success

Authorities haven't been standing still. A multi-agency operation involving the FBI, US Secret Service, and international partners announced 276 arrests this spring, alongside the evacuation of at least nine cryptocurrency fraud scam centers, many of which operate out of forced-labor compounds in Southeast Asia where the schemes' operators are themselves frequently trafficking victims. Operation Level Up's proactive victim notification effort has reached nearly 9,000 identified potential victims and is credited with saving an estimated $562 million in funds that would otherwise have been lost.

Even with those wins, investigators acknowledge the effort is only scratching the surface of the problem. Roughly 77% of victims contacted through Operation Level Up had no idea they were being scammed until authorities reached out directly, and researchers tracking the laundering side of the operation note that Chinese-language money laundering networks increased their share of known illicit crypto laundering activity to roughly 20% in 2025 alone, processing more than $16 billion, evidence that the financial infrastructure supporting these scams remains sophisticated and largely intact even as individual scam centers get shut down.
What Actually Helps

For anyone trying to protect themselves or a family member, the practical warning signs cluster around a consistent pattern: a new online relationship, often beginning through social media or a seemingly wrong-number text, that gradually and patiently steers toward a cryptocurrency investment opportunity, especially one showing suspiciously smooth, consistent gains. Financial fraud investigators consistently emphasize one practical safeguard above nearly all others: if someone you've never met in person is encouraging you to move money into a cryptocurrency platform they recommended, verify that relationship and that platform independently before sending anything, since by the time a withdrawal request gets denied, the money is typically already gone, laundered through multiple wallets within hours.

finance.title: The Justice Department Just Blew Up Its Own Offshore Tax Enforcement Playbook
finance.author: Maria Torres
finance.metaDescription: The DOJ dissolved its longstanding Tax Division and folded offshore enforcement into a new Fraud Division in 2026, reshaping how hidden money gets traced.

body.text: A Trail Across Borders, Now Under New Management

Tracing money hidden in offshore accounts has always depended on a specific kind of institutional muscle memory, investigators who understand the layered structures, shell entities, and treaty mechanisms that let money disappear across borders, and prosecutors who know how to turn that trail into a courtroom case. For years, that expertise lived inside the Department of Justice's Tax Division, a dedicated unit that built its reputation prosecuting exactly this kind of complex, cross-border financial concealment. In 2026, that institutional structure changed in a fundamental way.

On April 7, 2026, the Justice Department announced the creation of a new National Fraud Enforcement Division, a consolidated unit the department describes as laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting fraud against the American people. That reorganization effectively dissolved the standalone Tax Division as it had previously operated, folding its offshore enforcement responsibilities into a broader, fraud-focused structure that also handles healthcare fraud, COVID-relief fraud, and other categories of financial crime that previously sat in separate divisions.
Why This Reorganization Actually Matters

On paper, a reorganization chart might sound like a bureaucratic footnote. In practice, tax and financial crime attorneys describe it as a genuinely high-stakes reset for how the government pursues offshore tax evasion going forward. The prior structure, built around a dedicated Tax Division working in close coordination with the IRS, had developed real institutional depth over decades: IRS investigators brought financial and technical expertise, tracing intricate webs of offshore trusts and shell entities built specifically to obscure the true ownership of assets, while DOJ Tax attorneys brought the specialized prosecutorial and legal expertise needed to actually convert that financial detective work into successful criminal cases.

That symbiotic relationship produced real results over the years. A sustained offshore enforcement push in the 2010s led to numerous prosecutions of individuals and financial institutions that used offshore bank accounts to help clients evade US taxes, and the resulting wave of press releases, and the reputational and legal risk they signaled, is widely credited with driving many more taxpayers into the IRS's voluntary disclosure programs rather than risk prosecution. Whether a newly reorganized, broader Fraud Division can preserve that same specialized institutional depth while also handling a wider portfolio of general fraud cases is the open question now facing the department.
The New Division's Actual Casework

Since the reorganization, the National Fraud Enforcement Division has continued pursuing offshore-adjacent cases alongside its broader fraud mandate. In June 2026, the division announced the sentencing of a California man to 27 months in prison for tax evasion, operating an illegal offshore gambling business, and money laundering, a case that involved routing more than $4 million in income through a Costa Rica-based operation and laundering cash proceeds by exchanging them for checks made out to the defendant or his businesses. Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, now leading the consolidated division, announced the sentencing alongside federal prosecutors from the Central District of California, with the case explicitly framed as part of the department's broader Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

That case sits within a fuller docket of enforcement activity spanning far beyond offshore tax matters specifically, including health care fraud prosecutions, COVID-relief fraud cases, and money laundering conspiracies tied to drug trafficking organizations, evidence of just how broad the new division's actual caseload has become compared with the narrower, tax-specific focus of its predecessor.
The New Frontier: Offshore Money Meets Crypto

Layered on top of the institutional reorganization is a genuinely new complication for offshore enforcement: cryptocurrency. As digital assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum have gained mainstream popularity, including among organized criminal networks, they've opened up a new avenue for individuals looking to hide income and evade taxes, one built around decentralization and relative anonymity that traditional offshore banking structures never offered in quite the same way. The IRS has stated publicly that it remains committed to enforcing tax law in the digital asset space despite those unique technical challenges, but investigators acknowledge that tracing crypto-based concealment schemes requires meaningfully different tools and expertise than the traditional offshore trust and shell-company structures the department spent decades building institutional knowledge around.
What Comes Next for Anyone Hiding Money Offshore

For taxpayers weighing whether undisclosed offshore assets are still worth the risk, the practical message from enforcement attorneys hasn't really softened, even amid the institutional shakeup: the IRS continues issuing so-called John Doe summonses, court-authorized requests that compel offshore service providers to hand over records identifying US taxpayers who may have used their services to hide assets, a tool the agency has used repeatedly in recent years to identify targets before they're even aware they're under scrutiny. Whether that enforcement muscle proves just as effective operating inside a broader, more generalized Fraud Division as it did inside a dedicated Tax Division is likely to become clear only gradually, case by case, as the reorganized structure gets tested against the same complex, cross-border money trails it was always built to follow.

us.title: Google Found Guilty of Monopoly, Still Doesn't Have to Break Up
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: A federal judge ruled Google won't have to sell off its ad tech business despite finding it ran an illegal monopoly, the third failed Big Tech breakup bid.

body.text: A Guilty Verdict That Didn't Come With a Breakup

Google spent 2025 losing one of the most closely watched antitrust cases in recent tech history. This week, it avoided the punishment many expected to follow. US District Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled Wednesday that Google does not need to break up its advertising technology business, rejecting the Justice Department's request for exactly that kind of structural remedy, even though the same judge had already found in April 2025 that Google illegally obtained and maintained a monopoly over key parts of the online advertising market.

The Justice Department, joined by a coalition of state attorneys general, had specifically pushed for Google to divest AdX, its ad exchange where publishers pay the company a 20% fee to sell advertising space through instant, automated auctions. Brinkema declined, along with rejecting a separate proposal that would have forced Google to open-source the auction logic behind DoubleClick for Publishers, the ad server publishers use to manage what inventory gets sold.
What Google Gets to Keep, and What Actually Changes

Rather than ordering a breakup, Brinkema accepted most of the government's proposed behavioral remedies instead, changes to how Google operates its ad business rather than changes to who owns it. Those remedies reportedly include measures designed to push Google's ad tools to work more openly with competitors' tools, addressing the anticompetitive conduct the court already found, self-preferencing and unlawfully tying together different pieces of its advertising stack, without unwinding the underlying business structure.

The full details remain limited for now. Court officials said a complete ruling would follow within roughly two weeks, once confidential material is redacted, and both Google and the government have 30 days to file a joint proposed final judgment translating the judge's decision into specific, enforceable terms.
The Third Strike Against Big Tech Breakups

This isn't the first time federal courts have found a major tech company broke antitrust law and then declined to order a structural breakup as the fix. Google itself was separately found to have illegally monopolized the general internet search market in a related case, and in that matter too, the court stopped short of ordering the company be broken apart. A federal judge in Washington also rejected the Federal Trade Commission's attempt to force Meta to sell off Instagram and WhatsApp last year, finding the agency hadn't proven its social media monopoly claims to the court's satisfaction.

Taken together, legal observers describe a genuine pattern emerging in how US courts are handling Big Tech antitrust enforcement: judges are increasingly willing to find real anticompetitive conduct, but reluctant to impose the kind of structural change, forced sales, corporate breakups, ownership changes, that critics of these rulings argue is the only remedy capable of genuinely restoring competition once a dominant platform has already built its advantage.
Why the Stakes Go Beyond Just Advertising

Google's advertising technology stack might sound like a narrow, technical corner of its business, but the ad exchange at the center of this case runs the split-second auctions that decide which ad appears on which webpage, essentially invisible infrastructure that touches a huge share of the open internet's advertising revenue. A forced breakup could have meaningfully reshaped that market, and some analysts have noted a forced sale of Google's ad-tech assets could have specifically benefited rivals like Apple, which has been expanding its own advertising business, including recently working advertising into Apple Maps.

For a company simultaneously investing enormous sums into artificial intelligence, the ruling carries added significance beyond the advertising market itself. Google clearing another major legal threat with its core business structure and revenue engine intact means the company holds onto both the financial resources and the organizational continuity to keep funding its AI ambitions without the disruption a genuine corporate breakup would have caused.
What Happens Next

Google framed the outcome as validation of its own argument throughout the case, that a forced sale of AdX would be technically difficult to execute and would create a long, disruptive transition ultimately harming the publishers and advertisers who rely on the platform daily. Whether that argument holds up as more of the sealed ruling becomes public, or whether the Justice Department pursues an appeal once the final judgment is entered, remains to be seen. For now, the practical outcome is clear: Google keeps its advertising business fully intact, subject to new behavioral rules rather than a corporate breakup, extending a legal winning streak that's held through three of the biggest antitrust threats Big Tech has faced in years.

us.title: Uber's Biggest Layoffs Since the Pandemic: Robotaxis Are Why
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: Uber is cutting 3,300 jobs, nearly 10% of its workforce, its largest layoffs since COVID, as competition from Zoox and Tesla's Cybercab reshapes ride-hailing.

body.text: A Company at the Top of Its Game, Cutting Deep Anyway

Uber isn't struggling by any conventional financial measure. The company just wrapped its fifth consecutive year of 20%-plus annual gross bookings growth, joined the S&P 100 last September, and enters 2026 describing itself, in its own words to shareholders, as a scaled and profitable platform with substantial momentum. That backdrop makes Wednesday's announcement land differently than a typical layoff story: CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told employees the company is cutting roughly 3,300 jobs, close to 10% of its 34,000-person workforce, marking Uber's largest single round of job cuts since the COVID-19 pandemic.

Khosrowshahi framed the cuts around organizational structure rather than financial distress, telling staff the restructuring is meant to reduce layers of management and cut down on the organizational complexity that's been slowing the company's decision-making. Notably, he stopped short of blaming the cuts on artificial intelligence, a reason increasingly cited by tech executives across the industry when announcing workforce reductions this year.
The Robotaxi Threat Uber Can't Ignore

The more concrete pressure behind the timing is competitive, and it's coming from a direction Uber helped popularize but doesn't fully control: autonomous vehicles. Amazon's Zoox and Tesla's Cybercab are both expanding aggressively, raising real questions about whether the growing robotaxi industry could eventually challenge Uber's dominant position in ride-hailing, a business Uber has spent more than a decade building around human drivers as its core supply.

That's not a hypothetical risk Uber is ignoring. The company's own securities filings acknowledge the stakes directly, warning that failing to offer autonomous vehicle technology on its platform at competitive scale, or failing to do so before rivals get there first, could adversely impact its financial performance and future prospects. Uber has responded by investing substantial amounts of capital into partner companies developing autonomous vehicle technology, betting it can integrate AV partnerships onto its existing platform rather than get displaced by robotaxi operators running their own separate apps.
AI Spending Is Adding Its Own Kind of Pressure

Even as Khosrowshahi avoided directly blaming AI for the layoffs, Uber's own aggressive AI adoption appears to be straining the budget in a different way. According to media reports, Uber employees had exhausted the company's entire 2026 AI budget in just four months, evidence of how quickly AI tooling costs have been climbing across the tech industry even at companies actively trying to use the technology to become more efficient rather than simply cut headcount because of it.
A Bigger, More Complicated Year for Uber Overall

The layoffs arrive during an unusually active stretch for Uber's broader corporate strategy. The company has been pursuing a major international acquisition this year, structuring a takeover offer funded partly through existing cash and partly through a committed bridge financing facility worth roughly €14 billion, while separately pledging to invest €2 billion in Germany over the next five years covering local workforce development, business growth, and autonomous vehicle deployments in partnership with the German auto industry.

That combination, cutting thousands of domestic jobs while simultaneously committing billions of dollars to international expansion and autonomous vehicle infrastructure, captures the broader tension running through Uber's current moment: a financially strong company reorganizing itself not because the business is failing today, but because its leadership believes the ride-hailing industry's underlying structure is about to change, and wants Uber positioned to lead that change rather than get caught flat-footed by it.
What It Means for Uber Employees, and the Industry Watching Closely

For the roughly 3,300 employees affected, the immediate reality is straightforward and difficult regardless of the company's broader financial health. For the wider tech and gig-economy industry, though, Uber's move adds to a growing list of major companies restructuring their workforces in 2026 even while reporting strong core financial performance, a pattern that suggests the disruption many executives expect from AI and autonomous technology is shaping corporate decision-making well before it's fully reshaped the actual market these companies compete in.

us.title: Obama Presidential Center Welcomes Chicago Schools This Fall
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: The Obama Presidential Center launches school field trips this fall, months after its June 2026 opening drew tens of thousands to Chicago's South Side.

body.text: From Grand Opening to Everyday Use

The Obama Presidential Center spent its opening weekend in June drawing performances from Bruce Springsteen, Stevie Wonder, and U2's Bono, alongside tens of thousands of visitors who came to dance, play, and tour the new 19.3-acre campus on Chicago's South Side. This fall, the center is settling into a quieter but arguably more consequential phase of its mission: welcoming its first classes of local students for organized school visits, with reservations opening this semester for what the Obama Foundation describes as an educational program built to run for years to come.

The foundation is also continuing an unusually hands-on community outreach effort even months after the ribbon-cutting, an ongoing 77 Neighborhood Tour that's sending staff to coffee shops, festivals, and Chicago Public Library branches across every one of the city's official community areas. Stops scheduled for this week alone include the Garfield Ridge, Clearing, and Richard J. Daley library branches, part of a rolling schedule that's continued essentially nonstop since the tour launched earlier in the year.
More Than a Presidential Library

Visitors touring the completed campus this year have consistently noted that it doesn't function like a traditional presidential library. The site includes basketball courts, gardens, ball fields, a children's playground, and a full branch of the Chicago Public Library, wrapped around an eight-story museum tower that serves as the campus centerpiece. The first word visitors encounter walking into that museum, prominently displayed as one of the facility's numerous art installations, is simply hope.

That campus-style design was a deliberate choice. At the Grand Opening Ceremony in June, President Obama described wanting the center to function as a vibrant, living celebration of community, a space for learning, art, music, sport, and play built specifically to strengthen the bonds of trust that hold communities, and democracy, together. Michelle Obama echoed that framing in her own remarks, calling on attendees to choose hope as the center's animating idea.
A Long-Delayed Project, Finally Serving Its Neighborhood

The center's opening capped more than a decade of planning, community negotiation, and construction, with groundbreaking dating back to August 2021 and a total estimated project cost of roughly $850 million. Located at 6001 S. Stony Island Avenue in Jackson Park, the site sits squarely within the South Side neighborhoods the Obama Foundation has repeatedly emphasized as central to the project's purpose, rather than treating the center as simply a monument to a single presidency detached from the community physically surrounding it.

Most of the campus remains free and open to the public without requiring tickets, including the gardens, plazas, playground, and library branch; only the museum itself requires a timed-entry ticket, priced in line with other major Chicago museums and including designated free days for Illinois residents. That accessibility appears to be a deliberate extension of the same community-first framing the foundation applied to the center's design and opening celebration months earlier.
What Comes Next

With the ribbon-cutting now several months behind it, the center's real test is shifting toward the quieter, longer-term question of daily relevance: whether a campus built with this much civic ambition can actually become a lasting fixture of South Side community life, rather than a one-time cultural event that faded once the opening-weekend crowds went home. The launch of school programming this fall, timed deliberately to the start of the academic year, is one of the clearest signals yet that the Obama Foundation is treating that longer-term integration, not just the opening spectacle, as the project's real measure of success.

us.title: Gloria Steinem, Who Gave Feminism Its Public Face, Dies at 92
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: Gloria Steinem, the journalist and activist who became the face of second-wave feminism and co-founded Ms. magazine, died Wednesday at her New York home.

body.text: A Life That Helped Redefine What Women's Lives Could Look Like

Gloria Steinem, the journalist and activist whose name became nearly synonymous with the American feminist movement, died Wednesday at her home in New York City. She was 92. A statement posted to her official Instagram account said she passed away peacefully, surrounded by some of the many who loved her, adding that her near-century on earth were years well-lived, and that she continued working for equality until the very end.

Born in Toledo, Ohio, in 1934, Steinem graduated from Smith College in 1956 with a degree in government studies before spending two years in India on a fellowship, an experience she later credited with directly shaping the activism that would come to define the rest of her life.
The Story That Launched a Career

Steinem's path into journalism ran through an unlikely, deliberately provocative assignment. In 1963, she spent eleven days working undercover as a Playboy Bunny at a New York Playboy Club, an experience she turned into a two-part exposé for Show magazine that revealed grueling working conditions, mandatory medical exams, and pervasive harassment faced by the club's female employees. The piece made her a sensation, though she later said the fallout nearly derailed her career entirely, as editors afterward mostly offered her further undercover, semi-sexualized assignments rather than the serious political journalism she actually wanted to write.

By 1968, Steinem had become a contributing editor at the newly launched New York magazine, where she wrote a political column covering figures and issues including Shirley Chisholm's groundbreaking presidential run and New York's early fight over abortion rights. A 1969 piece she wrote connecting the women's liberation movement to the Black Power movement drew national attention and helped cement her role as one of the era's defining political journalists.
Building the Institutions the Movement Needed

Steinem didn't just write about the feminist movement, she helped build the institutions that carried it forward. In 1971, she co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus, aimed at increasing the number of women holding elected office. The following year, she co-launched Ms. magazine, the first major American publication owned, run, and written entirely by women, which became a defining outlet for feminist journalism and helped popularize the very language, including the term reproductive freedom, that the movement would use for decades afterward.

Ms. magazine's early willingness to tackle subjects other outlets avoided became part of its legacy in its own right; a 1972 feature in which 53 prominent American women, including Steinem herself, publicly stated they'd had abortions generated national conversation at a time when the topic was rarely discussed so openly in mainstream media.
A Public Life That Extended Well Into Her 90s

Steinem's activism never really slowed, even through a breast cancer diagnosis at age 52 that she caught early and successfully treated. In 2013, President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of the country's highest civilian honors, recognizing decades of advocacy for women's rights in the workplace, reproductive freedom, and political representation. Her life and influence were later depicted on screen in the FX miniseries Mrs. America, which streamed on Hulu in 2020.

In private life, Steinem became known for hosting what she called Talking Circles, informal gatherings that welcomed hundreds of guests into her home over the years, which she treated as an ongoing center for social justice organizing rather than simply a residence. She married David Bale, stepfather to actor Christian Bale, in 2000; he died of a brain tumor three years later.
How Those She Influenced Are Remembering Her

Tributes arrived quickly from figures across politics and culture. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton remembered Steinem as someone who pushed open doors not just for herself, but for millions of women who came after her, crediting Steinem's advocacy with paving the way for women's achievements Steinem herself never personally pursued, from space travel to competitive college athletics protected under Title IX. Actress and activist Meghan Markle, who described Steinem as a friend and mentor, wrote that privately, she was even better than anyone could imagine.

For a movement that Steinem spent more than half a century helping shape, both through her own writing and through the institutions she helped build, her death marks the loss of one of its most recognizable and enduring public voices, one who by most accounts never stopped treating the work as unfinished, right up until the very end.

us.title: Patagonia Is Suing Trump Over Utah's National Monuments. Again.
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: Patagonia and a coalition of tribes and environmental groups sued the Trump administration over July orders cutting two Utah national monuments by over 90%.

body.text: A Legal Fight That's Almost a Decade Old

Patagonia has sued a Trump administration over the same two Utah national monuments before, and this week, it did it again. The outdoor apparel company announced Wednesday it's joining a coalition of tribal nations and environmental groups in a new lawsuit challenging President Trump's July proclamations, which slashed Bears Ears National Monument by 91% and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument by 90%.

The scale of the reduction is stark in raw numbers. Bears Ears shrank from roughly 1.36 million acres to approximately 121,100 acres. Grand Staircase-Escalante went from about 1.87 million acres down to roughly 181,500 acres. Combined, the proclamations stripped protections from nearly 3 million acres of land.
The Legal Argument at the Center of the Case

Patagonia's lawsuit rests on a specific reading of the century-old Antiquities Act, the law presidents have used since 1906 to designate national monuments. The company and its co-plaintiffs argue the statute grants presidents the power to create monuments, but not the power to shrink or eliminate them once designated, a power they contend belongs to Congress alone under the Constitution.

The Trump administration and Utah's Republican Governor Spencer Cox have staked out the opposite reading. They argue the original monument designations themselves violated the Antiquities Act's requirement that protected areas be confined to the smallest area compatible with proper care and management of the specific objects being protected, meaning, in their view, correcting an overly broad designation falls squarely within a president's existing authority rather than requiring new legislation.
Land Sacred to Five Tribal Nations

Bears Ears carries particular significance beyond the legal question of executive authority. President Obama designated the monument in late 2016 following a proposal from five tribal nations, the Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation, and the Pueblo of Zuni, a coalition that has co-managed the monument alongside the federal Bureau of Land Management ever since. The lawsuit's supporters describe the site as containing thousands of Indigenous cultural and archaeological sites considered sacred to the tribes involved.

Patagonia CEO Ryan Gellert framed the administration's action in blunt terms in a statement posted to the company's website, calling the move illegal and describing the situation in Utah as tragic. Gellert also tied the dispute directly to Patagonia's own business interests, noting that public lands support the roughly $1.2 trillion outdoor recreation industry, a detail meant to underscore that the fight isn't purely symbolic for a company built around outdoor apparel and gear.
The Administration's Case for Shrinking the Monuments

The White House has defended the reductions as a matter of correcting government overreach rather than opening protected land to exploitation for its own sake. In public statements, administration officials have framed the move as righting the wrongs of past administrations by ending what they describe as abuse of the Antiquities Act, arguing the changes restore access and support what they call the economic and recreational lifeblood of Utah and the broader American West. Trump's proclamation itself cited the goal of putting the land to higher-priority use, including access to critical minerals the administration has tied to national security and resource independence.
A Rerun of the Same Fight, With Higher Stakes

This isn't new territory for either side. During Trump's first term in 2017, he issued similar proclamations shrinking Bears Ears by 85% and Grand Staircase-Escalante by nearly half, prompting Patagonia to become the first company ever to sue a sitting president over public lands. Those original lawsuits were ultimately shelved after President Biden restored both monuments to their original size in 2021, an outcome that effectively mooted the legal fight without ever producing a definitive court ruling on the underlying question of presidential authority.

This year's proclamations go considerably further than Trump's first-term versions did, which is part of why the case is drawing renewed attention. With the underlying legal question, whether a president can unilaterally undo a predecessor's monument designation, still formally unresolved after nearly a decade of on-again, off-again litigation, this new lawsuit may finally push a federal court toward a definitive answer, one that would likely shape how future presidents from either party can use, or reverse, national monument designations going forward.

us.title: NBA Slaps LA Clippers With a Record-Breaking $30 Million Fine
us.author: James Carter
us.metaDescription: The NBA suspended Clippers owner Steve Ballmer for a year and hit the team with a $30 million fine, the largest in league history, over Kawhi Leonard's deal.

body.text: A Record-Setting Punishment After a Year-Long Investigation

The NBA came down harder on a franchise this week than it ever has before. Following a nearly year-long investigation led by an outside law firm, the league announced Wednesday it was suspending Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer for one full year from all league and team activities, fining the team $30 million, the largest fine in NBA history, and stripping the franchise of five consecutive first-round draft picks, one in each year from 2029 through 2033.

The sanctions didn't stop with Ballmer. Clippers president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was banned for six months, and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended for a year without pay. Star forward Kawhi Leonard was fined $700,000 individually, though notably avoided any suspension or having his contract voided.
What the League Says Actually Happened

At the center of the case is a business relationship between Ballmer and Aspiration Partners, an environmental startup. The NBA found that Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities worth millions of dollars, and specifically approved a business deal he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement agreement with Leonard, according to the league's official findings. Investigative reporting from ESPN's Pablo Torre had previously described the arrangement as involving a $50 million investment Ballmer made in Aspiration that helped facilitate a $28 million endorsement deal for Leonard, one Torre characterized as a no-show arrangement that would violate the league's rules against circumventing the salary cap.

The NBA's findings went further still, describing the case as involving a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations by the Clippers organization, and specifically noting the franchise was a prior offender of the league's salary cap circumvention rules, language suggesting this wasn't treated as an isolated incident. As part of the league's own accounting, Leonard, acting through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, was found to have pressured the Clippers to help him secure those off-court opportunities and to have failed to reimburse the team for certain personal expenses.
Everyone Involved Is Denying Wrongdoing

The Clippers organization has rejected the league's conclusions outright, both before and after the punishment was announced. In a statement, the team said it vehemently rejects the NBA's findings, describing the investigation as heavily biased and accusing the league of seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than following the facts and evidence. The team had maintained throughout the year-long probe that it expected to be fully exonerated.

Leonard, for his part, issued a statement through his agent accepting responsibility for what he called lapses in judgment by people within his inner circle, while maintaining he personally entered into his contract and the related agreements in good faith, without knowledge that anyone intended to circumvent the salary cap. NBA Commissioner Adam Silver struck a starkly different tone, saying he was deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of league rules and the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures, adding that the severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations the investigation uncovered.
A Case Tangled Up With a Separate Fraud Scandal

The business partner at the center of the Clippers case has its own serious legal troubles entirely apart from the NBA investigation. Aspiration Partners co-founder Joseph Sanberg was sentenced earlier this year to 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to defrauding investors and lenders of at least $248 million, a case unrelated in its origins to the Leonard endorsement deal but one that added significant scrutiny to any business arrangement involving the company by the time the NBA's investigation concluded.
What This Means for Leonard's Future With the Team

The investigation's timing has been complicating an entirely separate piece of Clippers business. Leonard is reportedly expected to be traded to the Toronto Raptors, who agreed to a deal for him back in June, but that trade had been on hold pending the outcome of the league's investigation. With the NBA's findings and penalties now finalized, and with Leonard himself facing only a financial penalty rather than a suspension or voided contract, the long-anticipated trade appears positioned to move forward, even as the Clippers organization continues publicly disputing the findings that led to their record-setting punishment in the first place.

sports.title: Your Fantasy League Now Has an AI Assistant, Whether or Not
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: AI-powered draft assistants and daily audio briefings are now standard fantasy football tools in 2026, reshaping a market with 60 million US players.

body.text: From Draft Boards to Apps, and Now to AI

The fantasy football draft used to be a genuinely analog ritual: a printed cheat sheet, a stack of magazines, maybe a friend on the phone arguing about handcuff running backs. This year, heading into the 2026 NFL season, that ritual has quietly been rebuilt around artificial intelligence, with AI-powered tools now touching nearly every stage of a fantasy manager's season, from the draft itself through the weekly grind of waiver wires and start-sit decisions.

The scale of the audience these tools are now built for is genuinely enormous. The US fantasy sports market alone counts more than 60 million active players, the largest fantasy sports user base in the world, skewing heavily male, ages 18 to 35, with NFL fantasy football remaining the dominant format ahead of basketball, baseball, and hockey leagues.
What AI Actually Does Differently Than a Cheat Sheet

The specific tools proliferating this draft season fall into a few distinct categories, each solving a different piece of the fantasy puzzle. FantasyPros Coach AI has emerged as one of the more comprehensive options, layering AI-driven advice on top of the site's established rankings, projections, and real-time player data to generate advice tailored to an individual manager's specific roster and league settings, rather than generic, one-size-fits-all rankings.

Other tools have leaned into a different format entirely: daily audio briefings. Scoutcast.ai, for instance, generates a personalized two-minute audio rundown covering injury updates, waiver-wire targets, and matchup edges specific to a user's actual roster, layered on top of whichever platform, ESPN, Yahoo, Sleeper, or NFL.com, a league already runs on, rather than requiring managers to switch platforms entirely to access AI features.
The Chatbot Era of Fantasy Research

Perhaps the most visible shift is toward conversational, chat-based research tools that let managers simply ask a question in plain language rather than digging through spreadsheets and rankings pages themselves. RotoBot AI, one of the more prominent examples, handles queries spanning start-sit decisions, matchup history, injury impact, and usage trends across NFL, NBA, MLB, and several other sports, drawing on a live data pipeline of box scores, play-by-play logs, official injury reports, and sportsbook lines that updates continuously, including mid-conversation if betting lines move while a user is still asking follow-up questions.

That conversational approach extends into trade evaluation, too. FantasyPros' Trade Analyzer reviews a proposed trade against projected player performance and a team's specific roster needs, then assigns the deal a letter grade, giving managers, particularly newer ones less confident evaluating trade value on their own, a quick, defensible sanity check before hitting accept.
AI Betting Tools Are Blurring Into Fantasy Too

The line between fantasy sports and sports betting, always somewhat blurry, has gotten considerably blurrier this year as AI tools increasingly serve both audiences from the same underlying platform. Playbook, a tool integrated into the Action Network app as well as Twitter/X and Discord, lets users generate a pre-filled bet slip simply by tagging the tool under a pick or screenshot, reviewing the suggested slip before deciding whether to actually place it. Industry analysts tracking the space describe the bigger shift less as better math under the hood and more as better interfaces, AI tools have gotten meaningfully better at interpreting how bettors and fantasy managers actually communicate, shorthand picks, messy group-chat threads, screenshots, rather than requiring users to translate their thinking into a structured search query first.
A Market Consolidating Around a Handful of Platforms

Even as new AI tools multiply, the broader fantasy sports industry is consolidating around a smaller set of dominant platforms. DraftKings, FanDuel, ESPN, Yahoo, and Sleeper continue to lead the North American market specifically, expanding their reach through partnerships, AI-driven personalization features, and deeper integration with sports betting products, a trend industry analysts expect to continue through the rest of the decade as the underlying fantasy sports app market keeps growing at a double-digit annual rate.

For fantasy managers heading into draft weekend this year, the practical reality is that AI assistance is no longer a niche add-on for hardcore players willing to pay for premium research; it's increasingly baked directly into the free tier of the platforms millions of casual managers already use. Whether that actually makes leagues more competitive, or just gives everyone access to the same AI-generated advice and therefore cancels itself out, may end up being this season's most interesting unintended experiment.

sports.title: What Pro Athletes Actually Do to Recover, Beyond Ice Baths
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: NFL, NBA, and MLB athletes are turning to advanced recovery tech, from neuromuscular stimulation to pressurized chambers, to shrink injury recovery time.

body.text: What the Pros Actually Do, and It's Gotten Genuinely Sophisticated

For decades, professional athlete recovery meant a fairly predictable toolkit: ice baths, massage, basic electrical stimulation, and time. In 2026, athletes across the NFL, NBA, and MLB are investing in a considerably more sophisticated class of recovery technology, tools that target the nervous system, cellular repair, and sleep quality with a level of precision traditional sports medicine simply couldn't reach even a few years ago.

The shift isn't marginal or purely experimental. Enough professional athletes have adopted these tools, and reported compelling enough results, both anecdotal and measured, that some of the most recognizable names in their respective sports are now investing directly in the technology and the companies developing it, rather than simply using whatever equipment a team's training staff happens to provide.
Why Basic E-Stim Isn't Cutting It Anymore

Electrical stimulation has been a staple of physical therapy for decades, but the familiar twitch from a standard TENS unit barely scratches the surface of what the nervous system actually needs to rebuild after a serious injury, according to sports medicine specialists working directly with professional athletes. Traditional e-stim devices run on alternating current, a waveform that continuously reverses direction, which limits how deeply the signal can actually engage the neuromuscular system compared to newer technology built specifically for deeper, more targeted stimulation.

Dr. Sharif Tabbah, founder of Alkeme Sports Rx, has worked directly with multiple NFL players through ACL and Achilles recoveries, including Malik Nabers, Antonio Gibson, and other recognizable names, using next-generation stimulation devices as part of their rehab protocols. Tabbah described the difference as dramatic when measuring force output at intervals during a recovery period, saying his team sees noticeably faster strength gains in patients using the newer technology compared with those relying on standard e-stim alone.
A Broader Toolkit Than Just Better Electrical Stimulation

The newer generation of recovery tools extends well beyond neuromuscular stimulation alone. Athletes and training staffs are increasingly combining pressurized chambers, vibroacoustic therapy, and hyperbaric oxygen treatment into more comprehensive recovery protocols, often built around what industry coverage has described as five-in-one wellness machines that combine multiple recovery modalities into a single device rather than requiring athletes to cycle through separate pieces of equipment.

The underlying logic behind stacking these technologies together is straightforward: professional careers are short, injury risk is essentially constant given the physical demands of elite competition, and the practical margin between an athlete playing and not playing is often thinner than fans watching from the outside would assume. None of these tools eliminates that risk entirely, but for the athletes and medical staffs investing heavily in them, the goal is narrowing that margin as much as the technology currently allows.
The League-Level Version of the Same Idea

Individual athlete recovery technology is only half the picture. At the league level, the NFL's Digital Athlete program, a joint venture with Amazon Web Services, has taken a parallel but structurally different approach: rather than treating injuries after they happen, the system uses AI simulations processing roughly 500 million data points every week to forecast injury risk before it materializes as an actual torn ligament or fracture. All 32 NFL clubs now have access to a team portal showing daily training volume and injury risk data specific to their own roster, alongside league-wide benchmarks for comparison.

The results from that predictive approach have been measurable at a league-wide scale. AI-informed interventions and rule changes shaped by the program's data, including the 2024 Dynamic Kickoff redesign and the ban on hip-drop tackles, are credited with helping reduce lower-extremity injuries by roughly 25% across the league, a genuinely significant shift from treating injuries reactively toward what officials increasingly describe as engineered player availability.
Training the Institutions, Not Just the Athletes

Recovery technology adoption isn't limited to star players working with private specialists, either. The Professional Football Athletic Trainers Society, which represents NFL athletic trainers league-wide, has partnered directly with recovery technology company Hyperice to build formal education courses training current and future athletic trainers, including interns, on the latest innovations in recovery technology and player performance. That kind of institutional training pipeline matters because it means the newest recovery science doesn't stay confined to whichever star players can afford private specialists; it's meant to become standard practice across every NFL training room.

For amateur and recreational athletes watching from the outside, most of this specific technology remains genuinely out of reach, both in cost and in the kind of medical supervision it requires to use safely and effectively. But the broader principle behind it, treating recovery as an active, measurable, technology-assisted process rather than simply resting and hoping for the best, is increasingly filtering down into mainstream sports medicine and physical therapy more broadly, even if the exact tools professional athletes use remain, for now, well out of most people's price range.

sports.title: NFL Teams Are Now Worth More Than Some Countries' Entire GDP
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: NFL franchise values jumped 31% in a single year, with the Cowboys leading at $15 billion, as media rights, scarcity, and league rules keep pushing prices up.

body.text: More Than a Game, Considerably More

The NFL likes to sell itself as America's game, but by the numbers, it's just as accurately described as one of America's most valuable private industries. Heading into the 2026 season, the average NFL franchise is worth $7.1 billion, according to Sportico's annual valuations, after climbing an average of 31% in a single year, a jump that would be extraordinary for almost any asset class outside of sports team ownership.

The Dallas Cowboys sit at the top of the league, valued at roughly $15 billion, extending their long-running status as the most valuable franchise not just in the NFL but in professional sports globally. Across all 32 teams, the league now generates more than $23 billion in annual revenue, a figure that's climbed steadily even as the fundamental product on the field, 32 teams playing a 17-game regular season, has stayed essentially the same for years.
Where All That Money Actually Comes From

The single biggest driver behind these numbers is television. The NFL currently holds $110 billion in domestic broadcast rights spread across Amazon, CBS, ESPN/ABC, Fox, and NBC, a package that runs through 2032 but includes an opt-out clause the league can exercise starting in 2029. NBCUniversal alone pays roughly $2 billion a year for its NFL package, while Amazon Prime Video holds exclusive rights to Thursday Night Football, part of a broader shift toward streaming platforms bidding aggressively for NFL content alongside traditional broadcast networks.

That media money flows almost directly into franchise valuations. National revenue, driven overwhelmingly by those media deals, rose 5% to more than $450 million per club last year, and now accounts for roughly 62% of total team revenue leaguewide, according to Sportico's analysis. With the NFL actively exploring renegotiating its media contracts ahead of the 2026 season, and networks reportedly already signaling appetite for even higher valuations, team values are widely expected to keep climbing well beyond this year's already sharp increase.
Why NFL Teams Almost Never Actually Sell

Part of what makes NFL franchises such an unusual asset class is just how rarely they actually change hands. The Seattle Seahawks became just the fourth NFL team sold outright since 2015, following the Washington Commanders in 2023, the Denver Broncos in 2022, and the Carolina Panthers in 2018, a remarkably small number given how many other major asset classes turn over regularly. By comparison, twelve NBA teams changed hands over that same stretch, a stark illustration of how much more tightly held NFL ownership tends to be.

The Seahawks' sale followed the 2018 death of longtime owner Paul Allen, the Microsoft co-founder who originally bought the team for roughly $200 million back in 1997, a purchase price that looks almost quaint set against today's valuations. With no other NFL teams currently on the market, and the average ownership tenure sitting at 42 years, few analysts expect additional controlling-stake sales anytime soon, barring an unexpected event forcing an owner's hand.
The League's Own Rules Keep Prices Artificially High

Scarcity isn't accidental, it's partly engineered by the league's own ownership rules. The NFL requires a lead owner to hold at least 30% of a team, caps allowable debt during a sale at $1.5 billion, and prohibits ownership by sovereign wealth funds, corporations, or pension funds entirely. Private equity firms face their own restrictions, limited to 10% stakes and drawn from only a small, approved pool of firms, and debt isn't permitted on limited-partner interests at all.

Sports valuation expert Marc Ganis has described those restrictions as self-imposed governors on sale prices, noting pointedly that the league retains full authority to loosen any of them whenever it chooses, a lever that would likely push valuations even higher if the NFL ever decided to pull it. For now, those rules function as a deliberate ceiling on who's even eligible to buy in, which paradoxically helps drive up the price for the narrow pool of buyers who do qualify.
A Trend That's Bigger Than Just Football

The NFL's valuation surge isn't happening in isolation. The record for the highest change-of-control sale price for a US pro sports franchise was broken twice in 2025 alone, first when the Boston Celtics sold at an initial $6.1 billion valuation, then again three months later when the Los Angeles Lakers sold at $10 billion. If minority-stake sales are included, the New York Giants topped $10 billion in valuation terms when the Koch family purchased a stake in the team that September.

MLB and NHL franchises haven't reached quite the same stratospheric numbers, but they're tracking a similar upward trajectory: the Tampa Bay Rays sold for $1.7 billion this year despite ongoing uncertainty over their stadium situation, while the Minnesota Twins brought in new minority owners at a $1.75 billion valuation. One investment banking source told Front Office Sports that more than half of NBA and NFL teams have at least considered a minority-stake sale in recent years, a sign that even owners with no interest in giving up control are increasingly willing to cash out a slice of a franchise that keeps getting more valuable the longer they simply hold onto it.

sports.title: MLB's First Female Umpire Is Now Judged Like Everyone Else
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: A year after her historic debut, MLB's first female umpire Jen Pawol is now a full-time staff member in 2026, facing the same scrutiny as any other ump.

body.text: A Debut More Than a Decade in the Making

Jen Pawol handed her umpire's cap straight to a representative from the National Baseball Hall of Fame the moment her historic debut ended. On August 9, 2025, she became the first woman ever to umpire a Major League Baseball regular-season game, working first base for a doubleheader opener between the Miami Marlins and Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, a milestone that came after more than 1,200 minor league games spread across a decade-long career working her way up through the ranks.

Pawol, a former college softball player at Hofstra University, described the moment as something she was still absorbing well after the final out. It seemed like quite a few people were clapping and calling her name as she took the field, she told reporters afterward, calling the reception pretty intense and emotional. She's the seventh woman ever to work as a professional baseball umpire, and the first to reach MLB's regular-season roster in the sport's history.
From Historic Debut to Full-Time Big Leaguer

What's happened in the year since her debut is, in its own way, just as significant as the debut itself: Pawol has kept working. She returned to the majors that same August for a Pittsburgh Pirates-Colorado Rockies series, and by the 2026 season, she was working as a regular member of MLB's umpiring staff rather than a novelty one-off call-up, including serving as home plate umpire for numerous regular-season games throughout the year, a role that puts an umpire at the center of literally every pitch thrown in a game.

That shift, from a single history-making appearance to sustained, ordinary participation in the job, is arguably the more meaningful marker of progress. Barrier-breaking debuts generate headlines almost by default; what actually determines whether a barrier stays broken is whether the person behind it keeps getting the same opportunities, and faces the same expectations, as everyone else in the profession.
The Same Expectations Now Include the Same Scrutiny

That last part hasn't been entirely comfortable, and being covered honestly means acknowledging it. By mid-2026, statistical tracking site UmpScorecards, which grades every umpire's called balls and strikes against MLB's official Statcast strike zone, had Pawol posting a 91.8% overall accuracy rate and a 93.1% consistency rating for the season, with an accuracy-above-expected mark of negative 1.6%, numbers that placed her performance among the season's lower-ranked umpires by that particular metric. She was also involved in several high-profile games featuring contested strike-zone calls, including a rocky first inning during a June matchup between the St. Louis Cardinals and Minnesota Twins that drew heavy attention online.

It's worth being precise about what that scrutiny actually represents. MLB umpires across the league face exactly this kind of public, statistics-driven evaluation every season, a byproduct of pitch-tracking technology that's made every ball and strike call publicly reviewable in a way that simply didn't exist a generation ago. Pawol facing that same statistical spotlight, including the unflattering stretches, is in one sense the clearest sign yet that she's being treated as a working MLB umpire rather than a symbolic first, for better and for worse, in exactly the way any of her forty-some colleagues on the major league staff would be.
Part of a Broader Wave of Women in Baseball

Pawol's rise hasn't happened in isolation. Coverage of her debut at the time explicitly framed it as the latest milestone amid a broader surge of women taking on visible roles in professional baseball, spanning coaching staffs, front offices, and now, finally, the umpiring crew itself. She first broke a smaller barrier seventeen years before her regular-season debut, becoming the first woman to umpire a Spring Training game, a reminder of just how long a runway separated her earliest professional milestone from her ultimate arrival in the regular season.
What Her Second Year on the Job Actually Tests

Heading into the 2026 season's stretch run, Pawol's story has shifted from a single feel-good debut to a longer, messier, and in some ways more meaningful question: can she sustain a full career at the sport's highest level on the same terms as every other umpire, judged by the same metrics, facing the same criticism when calls go wrong, and getting the same opportunities for high-profile assignments when they go right. That's a considerably higher bar to clear than one celebrated afternoon in Atlanta, and it's the bar every genuine barrier-breaker in sports eventually has to clear if the barrier is going to stay down for the women who come after them.

sports.title: Tom Brady, Serena Williams, Billie Jean King Bet on New League
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: The NFL is launching a pro flag football league with TMRW Sports and investors like Tom Brady and Serena Williams, aimed at the 2028 LA Olympics.

body.text: A League Built Around a Single Deadline: 2028

The NFL announced in late March that it's partnering with TMRW Sports to launch a professional flag football league for both men and women, a move that ties together three separate storylines the league has been building toward for years: flag football's explosive grassroots growth, the sport's upcoming Olympic debut, and the NFL's own long-running effort to expand its footprint beyond the traditional 11-on-11 tackle game.

The timing isn't incidental. Flag football will make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, and the league's stated goal is to have its own professional competition up and running before that global spotlight arrives, giving elite flag players an actual professional stage to compete on in the years immediately before the sport reaches the Olympics for the first time in its history.
The Investor List Reads Like a Hall of Fame Ballot

NFL clubs voted at their December League Meeting to authorize 32 Equity, the league's collective investment vehicle, to put up to $32 million behind the new venture, but the money isn't coming from NFL ownership alone. The investor group backing the league includes an unusually star-studded roster: Pro Football Hall of Famers Peyton Manning, Joe Montana, Steve Young, and Larry Fitzgerald, alongside Tom Brady, Eli Manning, and current NFL players Arik Armstead, Bobby Wagner, and Russell Wilson. The group extends well beyond football, too, with Serena Williams, Alex Morgan, and tennis legend Billie Jean King also among the athletes who've bought in.

Institutional money followed the star power. Ariel Investments, Bessemer Venture Partners, Blue Pool Capital, Dynasty Equity, Silver Lake, and Sixth Street are all listed among the league's backers, a lineup that signals genuine financial conviction in flag football's commercial potential rather than a purely symbolic celebrity endorsement play.
Why TMRW Sports Specifically

The NFL selected TMRW Sports as its operating partner following a competitive process that drew interest from multiple potential operators. TMRW's track record made the pick easier to understand: the company previously built TGL, the primetime team golf league launched in partnership with the PGA Tour, giving it direct experience building a new made-for-television sports property essentially from scratch. NFL Executive Vice President of Football Operations Troy Vincent Sr. framed the selection as an important step in the league's long-term commitment to growing flag football, describing the new professional tier as completing a pathway that now runs from youth participation, through high school and college, up to the Olympic stage, and now to a genuine professional level.
The Growth Numbers Behind the Bet

The investment is backed by real participation data, not just enthusiasm. Roughly 4.1 million youth now play flag football in the United States, a jump of more than 50% since 2020, and the sport is now offered at the high school level in 39 states. The growth on the girls' side has been especially sharp: the number of young women playing flag football on their high school teams climbed nearly 60% between 2024 and 2025 alone, a trajectory that's helped make the women's side of the new professional league just as central to the league's plans as the men's.

That grassroots surge has already been visible at the exhibition level. The Fanatics Flag Football Classic in Los Angeles this past March put some of the sport's new star power on display directly, with Tom Brady tossing passes to Jalen Hurts as part of a showcase event, one of several high-profile flag football moments that have piled up in recent months as anticipation for the new league builds.
What the NFL Actually Gets Out of This

Beyond the Olympic angle, the league fits into a broader NFL strategy of using flag football as a lower-contact, more globally accessible entry point into the sport. NFL international leadership has previously described flag football's Olympic potential as a way to make football matter in countries that don't have deep tackle football traditions, part of the league's stated ambition to attract tens of millions of new international fans over the coming decade. A concussion-conscious sports landscape has also made flag football an increasingly attractive option for parents steering kids away from tackle football at younger ages, giving the NFL a version of its sport it can promote without the same safety concerns that have shadowed traditional football participation numbers in recent years.

No specific launch date for the league's first games has been announced yet, but with the investor group, operating partner, and financial backing now all in place, the remaining work is largely logistical: building out team structures, media deals, and a competitive calendar in time to have the league fully established well before the 2028 Olympic torch reaches Los Angeles.

sports.title: The WNBA's Newest Team Is Already One of the League's Best
sports.author: Sophie Nolan
sports.metaDescription: All eight 2026 WNBA playoff teams are set, with the expansion Golden State Valkyries locking in a second straight berth as the league's stingiest defense.

body.text: The Bracket Is Set, Weeks Before the Regular Season Even Ends

All eight teams for the 2026 WNBA playoffs locked in their spots well before the regular season wraps up on September 24, with the Dallas Wings clinching the final berth on the back of a win over Portland in which all five starters scored in double figures. The postseason field is set: Minnesota, Las Vegas, Golden State, Indiana, Atlanta, New York, Washington, and Dallas will all compete for the championship once the playoffs open on September 27.

The format keeps the pressure on from the very first game. All eight qualifying teams enter a seeded bracket with no first-round byes, playing best-of-three series in the opening round before the semifinals and WNBA Finals shift to a best-of-five format. Select games will air live on NBC and Peacock as part of the league's broadcast agreement, with the full bracket and television schedule finalized once the regular season concludes.
A Two-Year-Old Franchise Playing Like a Contender

The most compelling story heading into this postseason belongs to a team that didn't exist three years ago. The Golden State Valkyries clinched their second consecutive playoff berth, and this time they did it while sitting at 25-9, good for second place in the league standings behind the Minnesota Lynx. When the WNBA first announced the Valkyries as an expansion franchise back in 2023, owner Joe Lacob predicted the team would win a championship within its first five years, a bold claim for a franchise that didn't exist yet. Three seasons in, that timeline looks less like bravado and more like a plan that's actually on track.

The Valkyries already made history in their inaugural season, becoming the first WNBA expansion franchise ever to reach the playoffs in its first year of existence. This season, they've taken a genuine step further, winning more regular-season games, 23 through the stretch that clinched their berth, than any expansion team in league history had managed before, and building a roster that leads the WNBA in fewest points allowed per game, a defensive identity built without the kind of superteam roster construction that's defined other recent contenders.

Free-agent addition Gabby Williams, averaging 14.6 points and 1.6 steals per game, has emerged as one of the most impactful new pieces on any team in the league this season, a significant factor in the Valkyries' jump from first-year playoff surprise to genuine second-place contender.
The Fever Are Putting Up Numbers Nobody Else Can Match

Indiana's story this season has been about offensive firepower specifically. The Fever have topped 100 points in a WNBA-record 16 games this season, five more than any other team has managed in a single season in league history, securing their third consecutive playoff appearance in the process. That streak represents a genuine turnaround for a franchise that missed the postseason for seven consecutive seasons before finally breaking through in 2024.
A Rookie Making an Immediate Impact in Dallas

Dallas's path to the postseason has centered on a single standout performer. Paige Bueckers, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2025 draft, leads the Wings in both scoring and assists at 20.6 points and 5.8 assists per game, and scored 54 points combined over the two games in which Dallas clinched its playoff spot. It's Bueckers' first career playoff appearance, and it comes for a Wings team making its first postseason trip since 2023, giving Dallas one of the more compelling first-round storylines in a bracket that's otherwise dominated by more established playoff regulars.
Why This Season Matters for the League's Trajectory

This year's playoff race is unfolding against the backdrop of a league that's expanding rapidly. The 2026 season marks the WNBA's 30th year of existence and its largest footprint yet, growing from 13 to 15 teams with the addition of the Portland Fire and Toronto Tempo, following the Valkyries' own debut the year before. That kind of expansion typically comes with growing pains and diluted talent, at least in theory, which makes the Valkyries' rapid rise to genuine title contention a particularly useful data point for a league betting heavily on its continued growth: new teams, backed by real investment and smart roster building, can compete with the league's most established franchises almost immediately, rather than needing years to become competitive.
